title: Wages held back (James 5:1–6)
hookLine: the wages you withheld cry out

cards: Sundown at the edge of a harvested field. The reapers have been cutting grain since morning, and now they wait for the day's pay. No savings account.
No paycheck next Friday. The old law of Moses says why that pay can't wait: the worker is poor, and has set his heart on it. Tonight the owner says, come back next week.
That's the scene behind today's passage. And James, practical and plainspoken for four chapters, suddenly raises his voice.

teach.h: A VOICE LIKE THE OLD PROPHETS.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you." It sounds like the old prophets, Amos or Isaiah, thundering against injustice.
Then pictures of wealth rotting where it's stored: "Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten." The gold and silver, he says, have rusted, and the rust will be a witness against you.

Then the heart of it: "Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth."
The wages themselves cry out. Money that should have been in a worker's hand has a voice, and it reaches God.

Deuteronomy says to pay a poor laborer his wage on the same day, before the sun goes down, so that he doesn't cry to the Lord against you. James is drawing on that old command. And notice the title he uses for God.
Lord of sabaoth. It isn't sabbath. It's a Hebrew word meaning armies, or hosts.

teach.h: THE LORD OF HOSTS IS LISTENING.

teach.b: The commander of heaven's armies is listening to the cry of a farmhand who wasn't paid. Some churches teach from this passage that a fair wage, paid on time, isn't charity. It's justice.

how: Some churches draw on James 5 and Deuteronomy 24 in their teaching on fair wages and workers' rights, and some congregations make a point of paying their own staff and contractors promptly and fairly.

o: the Sabbath, the weekly day of rest
hosts or armies, as in the Lord of hosts
the harvest season, when wages came due

games.q: what's inside James 5:1–6 — tap the pairs.

s: Lord of sabaoth means Lord of the sabbath
sabaoth is a Hebrew word for armies or hosts. the Lord of hosts.
James says the cries of unpaid reapers reach the Lord
they "are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth."
James is drawing on an old command in the law of Moses
Deuteronomy says to pay a poor laborer on the same day.

games.q: you own fields. the harvest is in and the workers are waiting for their pay at sundown. cash is tight. what does the law James draws on say?
o: pay them next week when you've sold the crop.
pay them today, before the sun goes down.
games.why: Deuteronomy says the same day, before sundown. James says withheld wages cry out to the Lord of sabaoth.

practice: Think of the people whose work you depend on and rarely see: the person who picks your fruit, who cleans the office at night, who sews the clothes you're wearing.
Then think closer to home: do you owe anyone right now, a babysitter, a friend who covered lunch, a bill you've let slide? If you pray, you can pray for workers who are waiting on wages.

wordCard.voice: Sabaoth. Hebrew for hosts, armies, the Lord of hosts: the title James uses when he says a worker's unpaid wages cry out and reach God's ears.

orig.note: Hebrew: hosts, armies. carried into Greek as sabaōth, as in the Lord of sabaoth.
